## Implications for surveillance and management

Under SSP2-4.5 in 2041–2060, `r fmt(mg("245_2041-2060", "Australia", "Persistent (robust)"), 0)` × 10³ km²
of the current Australian range is classified as persistent (≥ 80% of GCMs),
`r fmt(mg("245_2041-2060", "Australia", "At risk (uncertain)"), 0)` × 10³ km² as at risk and
`r fmt(mg("245_2041-2060", "Australia", "Likely loss"), 0)` × 10³ km² as likely to be lost (@fig-surv,
@supptbl-mgmt). By 2081–2100 under SSP3-7.0, the persistent core shrinks to
`r fmt(mg("370_2081-2100", "Australia", "Persistent (robust)"), 0)` × 10³ km², and
`r fmt(mg("370_2081-2100", "Australia", "Likely loss"), 0)` × 10³ km² is likely to be lost. The persistent
core comprises coastal and highland New South Wales south of about 30°S, eastern and southern
Victoria and Tasmania. Robust emerging areas are very small
(`r fmt(mg("245_2041-2060", "Australia", "Emerging (robust)"), 1)` × 10³ km² under SSP2-4.5 2041–2060).
Climate change is therefore not projected to open substantial new areas to *H. longicornis* in
Australia. The surveillance gaps identified for current climate (`code_6`: Tasmania and western
Victoria) remain climatically suitable in all scenarios, except western Victoria, which is at risk
under higher emissions.

# Discussion

Projected with a model that demonstrably transfers between continents and with physically
consistent future predictors, climate change reduces the area climatically suitable for
*H. longicornis* in Australia. The range
contracts from its warm, dry margins in Queensland, inland New South Wales and Victoria, South
Australia and Western Australia towards a persistent core in south-eastern New South Wales, eastern
Victoria and Tasmania. The contraction is driven mainly by warming, and it scales with emissions in
the second half of the century. Gains are negligible. Previous projections reached
a qualitatively similar conclusion, but for largely artefactual reasons and with a much larger
apparent baseline range.

## Why the corrected projections differ from the previous analysis

The previous analysis reported contractions of 19–45%, similar in magnitude to those reported here
for Australia. The agreement is coincidental. The v2 model did not transfer between regions, and
its projected losses were driven by impossible aridity values and by a VPD approximation, not by
the temperature responses that govern tick development and survival. Its baseline range of
`r fmt(v2_cur_area / 1e6, 2)` million km² was `r fmt(v2_cur_area / area_true, 1)` times larger than that of the
validated model. It also included large areas of inland Australia where the tick does not occur and
which therefore could not be "lost". Its extrapolation was mostly produced by the aridity artefact,
and its ensemble was weighted towards high-sensitivity GCMs. The present projections remove each of
these problems: every predictor is computed from GCM output in the same way as the training data;
projected suitable area lies almost entirely within analogue climate; the GCM ensemble is screened
for climate sensitivity and model dependence; and the contributions of scenario, GCM and SDM to
uncertainty are quantified. The general lesson is that future projections are only as reliable as
the weakest derived predictor. Ad hoc scaling of derived indices is a common shortcut in SDM studies,
but it can move predictors outside their physical range without any visible warning.

## Mechanisms: heat and evaporative demand at the warm margin

The contraction follows directly from the fitted niche. Suitability in the consensus model is
unimodal in annual mean temperature, with an optimum of about 12–15 °C, and declines with aridity
and diurnal range (`code_3`, `code_6`). Much of the northern part of the current Australian range, in south-east
Queensland and northern New South Wales, already lies on the warm side of the optimum, so warming of
1–4 °C pushes it over the edge of suitable climate. Increasing evaporative demand reduces suitability
along the southern and inland margins, where moisture limits the range today. This is consistent
with the physiology of ixodid ticks: higher temperatures increase water loss and metabolic
costs of non-feeding stages, and desiccation during questing is a principal cause of mortality
[@needham1991; @ogden2016]. In the native range, *H. longicornis* is likewise absent from the
lowland subtropics of southern China, and in the cooler parts of its range it is limited by winter
cold. Tasmania and the Victorian highlands lie in the cool, humid part of the niche, so warming moves
them towards rather than away from the optimum, while the small increases in aridity there are not yet
limiting.

The contraction is not an artefact of extrapolation. All of the projected losses occur in climates
within the calibration range, which spans the native range in eastern and southern China and the
south-eastern United States, the latter including climates warmer than coastal Queensland. Novel
climates occur only in the tropical and arid north, where the tick is absent and suitability is
far below the threshold. Clamping, which affects only those areas, cannot alter the conclusions.

## How much has already changed

Because the model was trained on 1970–2000 climate, part of the projected contraction, about a
tenth of the Australian range by 2021–2040, represents change that has probably already happened.
This has two practical implications. First, records from the 1970s–1990s at the northern margin of the
range in Queensland may describe populations that are now climatically marginal, and current tick
burdens there may already be lower than historical records suggest. Second, the hindcast offers a
test of the model: if surveillance in the margins finds declining tick abundance or prevalence of
*T. orientalis* infection since the 1990s, this would support the projections.

## Uncertainty and what would reduce it

For decisions over the next few decades, the main uncertainty is which GCM best represents the
regional climate, not the emissions pathway. The pathways diverge only after mid-century, when they
become the dominant source of uncertainty. SDM uncertainty contributes a moderate and fairly
constant share. This pattern means that improving the representation of regional climate, for example
by weighting GCMs by their skill over eastern Australia [@knutti2017; @grose2020] or by using
regionally downscaled projections, would narrow near-term projections more than refining the SDM.
For the end of the century, the projections are better framed as conditional on emissions: in
Australia, roughly a fifth of the suitable area is lost under strong mitigation and almost half under
very high emissions.

## Implications for biosecurity and livestock industries

Three messages follow for management. First, the core of the tick's range, which carries most of the
affected dairy and beef cattle in south-eastern Australia, remains climatically suitable under every scenario. *H. longicornis* and *T. orientalis* will
remain a long-term problem there, and control programmes should be planned on that basis. Second,
the northern and inland margins of the Australian range are likely to become less suitable,
starting now. Investment in long-term tick control infrastructure in those areas should account for
declining climatic suitability. Monitoring there would also show whether the tick is retreating as
projected. Third, climate change is not projected to open new areas, so the surveillance priorities
identified under current climate, mainly Tasmania and western Victoria, remain the priorities. Their importance rests on introduction risk through stock movement,
not on climatic expansion.

## Limitations

The projections inherit the limitations of the current-climate model: they describe climatic
suitability at about 5 km resolution and ignore microclimate, vegetation, irrigation and host
density, all of which can sustain populations in marginal regional climates. Irrigated pasture and
riparian refugia within the *likely loss* areas may allow the tick to persist locally. The model
assumes that the climatic niche will be conserved and that populations cannot adapt to warmer
conditions within the projection horizon. The niche analysis in `code_3` supports conservatism across
the invasion, but it cannot rule out adaptation. Projections are equilibrium suitability, not
predicted occupancy: they say nothing about the rate at which populations decline at the margins.
Future predictors are WorldClim delta-downscaled CMIP6 monthly climatologies, which represent
changes in mean climate only, not changes in variability or extremes such as heatwaves and droughts,
which may matter more for tick survival. Finally, the aridity index uses the temperature-based
Hargreaves equation for PET, which may overestimate increases in evaporative demand under warming
compared with physically based formulations. This would make the projected moisture-driven losses
conservative upper bounds.

## Conclusions

Corrected and re-run with a transfer-validated model, the projections show that climate change will
contract the range of *H. longicornis* in Australia from its warm and dry margins, by about a tenth
already and by a fifth to almost a half by the end of the century depending on emissions. The core
range in south-eastern Australia and Tasmania will remain suitable. Warming is the main
driver; projected losses lie entirely within analogue climates; and the GCM is the main source of
uncertainty until mid-century. The previous projections reached superficially similar numbers through
a model that did not transfer and through physically impossible future predictors, and they should
be replaced by those presented here.

# Extending the analysis to increase its practical impact

The projections answer the question "where will climate permit *H. longicornis* to persist?". Managers
and industry need answers to "where, when and with what consequences will the tick and its
pathogens affect animals and people, and where should we act?". The extensions below are ordered
roughly by the ratio of impact to effort. Several reuse the outputs of this analysis directly
(suitability, agreement and change-class rasters in `processed_data_7/`; scenario summaries in
`outputs_7/`). The Australia-only implementation of extensions 1–5 and 7 is in `code_8/`.

**1. Convert suitability into exposure of livestock (high impact, low effort).** Overlaying current
and projected suitability on cattle (beef and dairy) and sheep densities would translate area into
animals at risk. Suitable sources are the Gridded Livestock of the World [@gilbert2018], ABS
agricultural census data for Australia. Combined with
*Theileria orientalis* Ikeda case data and published production losses, this would give projected
economic exposure by region and scenario, the metric that industry bodies and governments use to
prioritise investment.

**2. Add introduction pressure to identify where establishment is most likely (high impact).**
Climatic suitability is necessary but not sufficient for establishment. Livestock movement records
(the National Livestock Identification System, NLIS) could be used to estimate the rate at which ticks are moved
from infested areas into the *emerging* and *persistent, unrecorded* areas identified here. Wildlife
hosts (deer, macropods, hares) and birds should be considered as well. Combining introduction pressure
with suitability would produce establishment-risk maps for targeting movement controls,
pre-movement treatment and surveillance, in particular for Tasmania.

**3. Move from presence to abundance and seasonality with a process-based model (high impact,
moderate effort).** Losses and gains of suitable area do not show whether tick burdens or the timing
of activity will change in the core range, where most animals are. A stage-structured population
model driven by temperature-dependent development and moisture-dependent survival
[@needham1991; @ogden2016], parameterised from laboratory and New Zealand field data, could project the
number of generations, the length of the questing season and relative abundance under the same
scenarios. Such a hybrid correlative-mechanistic approach [@kearney2009] would also give an
independent check on the correlative projections in climates outside the calibration range, and it
would support practical advice on the timing of acaricide treatment and stock management.

**4. Represent the fine-scale refuges that decide persistence at range margins (moderate effort).**
At 5-km resolution the model cannot represent irrigated pasture, riparian vegetation or cool, moist
gullies. These are likely to sustain populations where regional climate becomes marginal, for
example on irrigated dairy land in northern Victoria and along the inland slopes of the Great
Dividing Range. Adding land-cover and irrigation layers, and using 1-km or regionally downscaled
projections (NARCliM2.0 for south-eastern Australia), would
make the predicted *likely loss* areas more realistic, because these areas are where coarse
climate surfaces are least representative.

**5. Report results by global warming level (low effort).** Expressing projections at 1.5, 2 and 3 °C
of global warming, rather than by SSP and period, separates the question of how much warming will
occur from the question of what a given amount of warming does to the tick. This aligns the results
with policy targets and national climate services, and it reduces sensitivity to which GCMs are
included [@hausfather2022]. GCM-specific warming levels can be assigned to each GCM × SSP × period
combination already computed here.

**6. Validate the projections with independent and temporal data (moderate effort).** Hindcasting
the documented spread of the tick in Australia over the twentieth century, and its
spread in the eastern United States since 2017, would test whether the model predicts change over
time and not just pattern in space [@yates2018]. Structured surveys in the predicted emerging and
at-risk areas would provide true absences, which presence-only models lack.

**7. Design surveillance explicitly (high impact for biosecurity agencies).** The management
categories in @fig-surv can feed a formal surveillance design: allocating sampling effort among
*emerging* and *persistent, unrecorded* areas to maximise the probability of early detection for a
given budget, using sentinel herds, veterinary and abattoir submissions and citizen-science
reports. Each new detection or confirmed absence can then update the model, so that the maps
improve as surveillance proceeds.

**8. Extend to pathogens.** *H. longicornis* is a competent vector of several
pathogens of animal and human health importance [@zhao2020]. Combining tick suitability with
pathogen-specific surveillance (*Theileria orientalis* genotypes, and screening for exotic
bunyaviruses and rickettsiae) would give One Health risk maps for Australia.

**9. Strengthen the model itself.** Three improvements would reduce uncertainty, and the variance
partitioning shows where reductions matter most: (i) adding further algorithms (e.g. GAM, boosted
regression trees) to capture algorithmic uncertainty; (ii) weighting GCMs by their skill over
Australia and their independence [@knutti2017]; and (iii) testing whether
parthenogenetic and bisexual lineages differ in climatic niche, because invaded populations are
parthenogenetic. Reporting the model with the ODMAP protocol [@zurell2020] and publishing the rasters
through an interactive map would make the results easier for agencies to adopt.

# Supplementary material {.appendix}

## Supplementary tables

::: {.supp-table}
::: {#supptbl-v2}
| # | Component | What the previous analysis (v2, `code_2` Steps 8–10) did | Why it is a problem | What this analysis does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Model projected | Projected the v2 MaxEnt model (BIO2, BIO3, BIO13, aridity, VPD; stepwise-VIF selection, no absolute temperature variable, LQH features). | The v2 model did not transfer between regions under current climate: leave-one-region-out AUC was `r fmt(v2_loro$auc[v2_loro$region == "Oceania"])` for Oceania, `r fmt(v2_loro$auc[v2_loro$region == "East_Asia"])` for East Asia and `r fmt(v2_loro$auc[v2_loro$region == "North_America"])` for North America (0.5 = random). A model that cannot transfer in space cannot be trusted to transfer in time. Warming entered only through proxies (VPD, isothermality), and the model predicted `r fmt_int(v2_cur_area)` km² currently suitable, `r fmt(v2_cur_area / area_true, 1)` times the area predicted by the validated model. | Projects the transfer-validated consensus (`code_3`), which includes annual mean temperature in every member and reproduces the Oceanian distribution when trained without Oceanian records. |
| 2 | Future aridity, PET and CMI | Scaled current ENVIREM values by the ratio of future to current BIO1 in °C (denominator floored at 0.1 °C; absolute value taken) and by the ratio of future to current precipitation. | Ratios of Celsius temperatures have no physical meaning: the same 2 °C warming multiplies "PET" by 1.1 at 20 °C and by 21 at 0.1 °C, and sign changes are lost. The aridity index (bounded at 100) exceeded 100 in `r fmt(v2_ai_stats$pct_above_100[v2_ai_stats$id == "MPI-ESM1-2-HR_ssp245_2041-2060"], 0)`% of Australian land under MPI-ESM1-2-HR SSP2-4.5 2041–2060 and in `r fmt(v2_ai_stats$pct_above_100[v2_ai_stats$id == "ACCESS-CM2_ssp585_2081-2100"], 0)`% under ACCESS-CM2 SSP5-8.5 2081–2100 (maximum `r fmt(v2_ai_stats$max_v2[v2_ai_stats$id == "ACCESS-CM2_ssp585_2081-2100"], 0)`). These impossible values put most of the projection domain outside the calibration range, which accounts for much of the 60–81% extrapolation reported. | Computes aridity from each GCM's monthly temperature and precipitation with the ENVIREM formulation (Hargreaves PET), applied as an anomaly to the training layer (@suppfig-validation). |
| 3 | Future VPD | Current CHELSA VPD × exp(0.06 ΔT). | Saturation vapour pressure scaling only; ignores changes in relative humidity, which differ among GCMs and dominate VPD change in drying regions. | VPD is not a predictor in the consensus. If needed, GCM-specific CHELSA-CMIP6 VPD should be used. |
| 4 | Baseline consistency | Documentation states ENVIREM variables were recomputed from WorldClim 2.1; the code loads the published ENVIREM layers, which are built on an earlier WorldClim baseline. | Future change computed against one baseline was applied to layers built on another. | Change is computed between WorldClim 2.1 current and future monthly climate with an identical formulation, then added to the training layer. |
| 5 | GCM ensemble | Five GCMs (ACCESS-CM2, CNRM-CM6-1, MIROC6, MPI-ESM1-2-HR, UKESM1-0-LL), chosen without stated criteria. | Three of the five have ECS > 4.5 K, and UKESM1-0-LL (≈ 5.3 K) lies outside the IPCC AR6 very likely range, so the ensemble is warm-biased for any SSP [@hausfather2022]. Five members give a coarse estimate of spread. | Ten GCMs selected for data completeness, ECS within 2–5 K and independence (@tbl-gcm). The v2 ensemble and a likely-ECS subset are compared as sensitivity analyses. |
| 6 | Scenario design | SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5; 2041–2060 and 2081–2100. | No near-term period (2021–2040), which is the most relevant to current planning; no low-emission pathway; SSP5-8.5 was the only high-end scenario, although it is now considered an unlikely trajectory [@hausfather2020]. | Four SSPs (1-2.6, 2-4.5, 3-7.0, 5-8.5) × four periods (2021–2040 to 2081–2100). |
| 7 | Suitable area | Cell count × a single cell area evaluated at the mean latitude of the 8–48°S extent. | Cell area is about one-third smaller at 48°S than at 8°S. With suitable climate concentrated in the south, this overestimates suitable area (by `r fmt(100 * (area_v2_approx / area_true - 1), 0)`% for the current consensus map). | True latitude-dependent cell areas. |
| 8 | Threshold | Maximum sensitivity + specificity threshold. | Inconsistent with the threshold used for current-climate reporting in `code_3`; change estimates depend on the threshold. | 10th-percentile training-presence threshold, as in `code_3`; MSS reported as a sensitivity analysis. |
| 9 | Extrapolation | MESS computed and binary maps masked for MESS < 0, but range-shift statistics were computed from unmasked maps. Univariate MESS only; clamping not assessed. | Inconsistent treatment; novel combinations of individually analogue values were ignored. | MESS and ExDet NT2 for every scenario; clamped vs unclamped predictions; suitable area reported with and without novel climates. |
| 10 | Ensemble summary | Binary map from the median of continuous suitability; GCM agreement shown for SSP5-8.5 2081–2100 only. | The area of the median map is not the median of the areas, and agreement in one scenario says nothing about the others. | Per-GCM binary maps; area statistics as median and range across GCMs; agreement and change classes for every SSP × period. |
| 11 | Uncertainty | GCM spread only. | SDM (parameter) uncertainty, often the largest component [@buisson2010], was ignored, and uncertainty sources were not compared. | Bootstrap SDM replicates × GCMs × SSPs; ANOVA partitioning of uncertainty for every period. |
| 12 | Interpretation | No attribution of change to climatic drivers; "priority surveillance" areas defined from SSP5-8.5 2081–2100 only. | It was unknown whether projected losses were driven by warming or by the artefactual moisture variables; surveillance priorities were based on the least policy-relevant scenario. | Temperature-only and moisture-only projections, single-variable attribution and dominant-driver maps; management categories for SSP2-4.5 2041–2060 and SSP3-7.0 2081–2100. |
| 13 | Reproducibility | Hard-coded absolute paths that do not match the project location; MESS calculated with different functions in Steps 6 and 9. | Code does not run as written; current and future extrapolation were not strictly comparable. | Paths relative to the project; one MESS implementation, validated against `code_3`. |

Problems identified in the previous future-climate analysis, their consequences, and the corrections made here.

```{r}
  as.data.frame(aggregate(to_rast(ens_maps[[k_s]]$sd), 2, mean, na.rm = TRUE), xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE) |> mutate(src = "Among climate models (GCM SD)"),
  as.data.frame(aggregate(to_rast(sdm_sd[[k_s]]), 2, mean, na.rm = TRUE), xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE) |> mutate(src = "Among SDM bootstrap replicates (SD)")) |>
  ggplot() + geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = value)) + geom_sf(data = aus_sf, fill = NA, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = "SD of\nsuitability", limits = c(0, NA)) + facet_wrap(~ src) + map_base
save_fig("FigS9_uncertainty_SSP245_2041-2060", w = 12, h = 6)
```
Standard deviation of projected suitability among GCMs and among SDM bootstrap replicates for SSP2-4.5 2041–2060 (compare @fig-uncert b).
